raw: {"slots": {"question": [{"claim": "The paper asks how partisan polarization in online COVID-19 discourse varied across subnational regions and over time in the United States and Canada. To answer this, it proposes a new computational way to measure such variation.", "quotes": [{"text": "This study introduces a novel computational approach to measure subnational and event-driven variation in partisan polarization and explores these dynamics across the United States and Canada.", "page": 1}]}, {"claim": "Specifically, it asks whether polarization correlates with three things: a region's ideological leaning, the volume of conspiracy-related content, and vaccination rates.", "quotes": [{"text": "we analyze millions of tweets to determine how polarization correlates with: (1) the ideological leanings of different regions; (2) exposure to conspiracy theory-related content; and (3) vaccination rates.", "page": 3}]}], "central_claim": [{"claim": "Conservative regions in both countries showed higher partisan polarization in pandemic discourse, and the effect was stronger in the United States.", "quotes": [{"text": "Our analysis reveals that politically conservative regions exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization in both countries, with this effect particularly pronounced in the United States.", "page": 1}]}, {"claim": "Polarization was not uniform. It varied by geography, political leaning and public-health topic, and it differed substantially between the two countries.", "quotes": [{"text": "we have demonstrated that polarization is not uniform but varies significantly by geography, political leaning, and public health topic, with substantial differences between the two countries.", "page": 25}]}], "evidence": [{"claim": "The data are COVID-19 political tweets collected from October 2020 to January 2021: about 12.5 million linked to the US and 46.6 million linked to Canada. Users were geolocated and classified by party affiliation.", "quotes": [{"text": "We collected a large-scale dataset of COVID-19 political discussions on Twitter (now X) occurring between October 9, 2020, to January 4, 2021, comprising approximately 12.5 million tweets linked to the United States and 46.6 million tweets linked to Canada.", "page": 4}]}, {"claim": "Polarization is measured as the separation between left- and right-leaning users' language in a RoBERTa embedding space, using a C-index clustering measure. The measure is computed separately by topic (lockdowns, masks, vaccines), region and time.", "quotes": [{"text": "We then measure polarization by quantifying how far apart the language of left and right-leaning users is positioned in this embedding space, using the C-index [42], a robust clustering measure.", "page": 4}]}], "key_findings": [{"claim": "In the US, a state's Republican vote share correlated significantly with polarization on masks and vaccines, but not on lockdowns.", "quotes": [{"text": "We find strong, significant correlations in the US between Republican vote share and polarization around masks and vaccines, though not for lockdowns.", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "Across US states, vaccine-related polarization was strongly and negatively correlated with vaccination rates measured a year later.", "quotes": [{"text": "we confirm a strong negative correlation (r = −0.77, p < 0.001) between vaccine polarization and vaccination rates.", "page": 16}]}, {"claim": "Polarization spiked around specific events, rising and decaying symmetrically over a few days.", "quotes": [{"text": "This aggregate analysis (Fig 14c) confirms a rapid, symmetric rise-and-decay profile around polarization peaks, occurring on timescales of days.", "page": 19}]}, {"claim": "Conservative partisans in both countries posted more conspiracy-related content.
